summary: Defines the profile link relation type, which lets a representation indicate that it follows one or more profiles. A profile does not change the meaning of the representation but tells clients about extra constraints, conventions or extensions. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A label on a box that says how it is packed, so you know the extra rules for opening it, though the box is the same box.

subtitle: How to label representations with additional constraints and conventions beyond their media type.

tldr.problem: A resource's media type tells you what kind of thing it is, but sometimes you need to indicate extra rules, conventions or extensions that a client should know about.
tldr.mechanism: The profile link relation type allows representations to reference one or more profiles using a URI identifier. A profile does not change the basic media type semantics, but signals additional processing rules that clients aware of the profile can follow.
tldr.outcome: Clients can discover and adapt their behavior to profiles, allowing the same media type to represent different specializations without creating entirely new media types.

facts.label: Profile combinations
facts.value: A resource can link to zero or multiple profiles

today: RFC 6906 is an Informational RFC that remains active. The profile link relation is now widely used in web APIs, feeds, and semantic web applications to annotate representations with additional processing rules.

sections.title: Profiles and Media Types
sections.content:
Every resource sent over the web is labeled with a media type (like text/html or application/json) that tells a client how to parse and understand it. Sometimes, however, a specific instance of a media type follows additional conventions or constraints beyond what the media type definition alone specifies. A profile is a way to signal these additional semantics without creating a new media type.

For example, HTML has always supported a profile attribute in the head element, but this mechanism was specific to HTML. RFC 6906 generalizes profiles to work with any media type by defining the profile link relation type.
sections.eli5: You know a box is a box by looking at it, but a sticker says 'this box contains a birthday gift' or 'this box is fragile', which tells you extra rules for handling it.

sections.title: What a Profile Is
sections.content:
A profile is a set of additional semantics that can be applied to a resource representation, such as constraints, conventions, or extensions. Critically, a profile MUST NOT change the basic meaning of the representation when processed without profile knowledge. This means a client that does not understand a profile can still safely use the representation; it just will not benefit from the extra semantics.

Profiles are identified by URI. Like XML namespace URIs, the profile URI serves primarily as an identifier; clients SHOULD treat it as a stable identifier rather than automatically dereferencing it. However, profile maintainers MAY make the profile URI dereferenceable and provide documentation at that URI for clients that want to understand the profile.
sections.eli5: A profile is extra rules that do not change what the thing fundamentally is, so a reader who ignores the profile still gets the core meaning right.

sections.title: Profiles Versus New Media Types
sections.content:
The distinction between a profile and a new media type comes down to whether additional semantics layer on top of an existing media type or completely redefine it. For example, hCard is a profile of HTML because it adds processing rules to extract vCard contact information from HTML structures without changing how HTML itself is parsed. By contrast, XHTML is a new media type because it presents a completely new perspective on XML structures.

Media types that may be used with profiles SHOULD define a media type parameter called profile so clients can request a specific profile (for example, in an HTTP Accept header). The profile link relation complements this parameter by making the profile explicit within the representation itself.
sections.eli5: If you are just adding extra rules on top of HTML, that is a profile. If you are completely redesigning how things work, that is a new media type.

sections.title: Profile Examples
sections.content:
The hCard profile (http://microformats.org/profile/hcard) allows vCard information to be embedded in HTML using microformats. The Dublin Core profile (http://dublincore.org/documents/2008/08/04/dc-html/) embeds Dublin Core metadata in HTML using link elements.

Podcasts extend feed formats with podcast-specific fields for audio and video metadata. A podcast-aware feed reader can use the podcast profile to offer specialized UI and features, while a generic feed reader can still parse the basic feed. These examples show how profiles let servers and clients agree on conventions without requiring new media types.
sections.eli5: hCard says 'this HTML has hidden contact info', Dublin Core says 'this HTML has metadata tags', and podcasts say 'this feed has audio and video extras'.

sections.title: Registration and Usage
sections.content:
The profile link relation type is registered with IANA as a standard web linking mechanism. It can be used in HTTP Link headers, in representations that support typed links (such as Atom feeds or HTML documents), and in media type parameters.

When using the profile link relation, clients SHOULD NOT indiscriminately dereference profile URIs, as profiles serve as identifiers and dereferencing may not always be useful or appropriate. Profile URIs are typically opaque identifiers that tell clients to apply certain processing rules or constraints.
sections.eli5: The profile link is now an official web standard, registered in IANA's link relation type registry, so anyone can use it.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The profile link relation type does not introduce new security issues beyond those already discussed in RFC 5988 (Web Linking). Profiles are identifiers and do not inherently carry code or executable content. The security of profiles depends on the same mechanisms used for general web linking, such as HTTPS and signed links where appropriate.

Server and client implementations should validate that profile URIs are from trusted sources before changing behavior based on them, just as with any external identifier.
sections.eli5: Profiles are just names, not code, so they are as safe as any other web link.
